meta.notes: Primary ICP from context is US working adults reached via employer caregiver benefits, so 5c prospects are US employers/insurers that already buy a caregiving benefit (they evidence the B2B2C buyer but are already served by Wellthy/Cariloop/Bright Horizons). Only 16 prospects found (target was 20+); only 3 have a named contact on their own pages; no size estimates recorded because no company's own page stated headcount. Several useful sources were unfetchable by Preuve (care.samarth.community and reddit via robots.txt, NCBI/PMC, caring.com, caringvillage.com, Columbia/Harvard/Wellesley HR pages) and were left out. A widely repeated '2024 ASHA survey' NRI statistic appears only on a vendor blog and was not used. No public evidence found for CareZone's shutdown (founder-listed risk), for Hera, or for Samarth (site blocks crawler). Apollo NRI 360 prices are shown without a billing period.

summary.statement: NRI families coordinate parents' care mainly through family WhatsApp groups, a designated local relative or neighbour, and phone calls; medical reports are shared as PDFs in the group.
Providers and guides describe the WhatsApp approach as fragmented: information arrives in pieces and relatives interpret updates differently.
Families who need more hire paid care managers (Emoha, Anvayaa, Apollo NRI 360) whose plans already include an app or helpline for children abroad.
No source quantifies how many NRI families use a dedicated coordination app; one operator says most parents won't go beyond WhatsApp.
Triggers named for buying paid help are a fall, a hospitalisation, cognitive decline, or remote self-management becoming unsustainable.
Families with a nearby sibling or a working local network are advised they probably don't need a paid service.
These triggers lead to buying hands-on services (care managers, attendants), not standalone coordination software; no evidence shows a software-only purchase trigger.
Indian elder-care service subscriptions run about Rs 5,000-25,000 per month; Emoha's plans are Rs 1,999-10,999 per month.
A live-in attendant costs about Rs 15,000-50,000 a month and basic care Rs 15,000-30,000, often paid by the NRI from an NRO account.
Apollo NRI 360 is priced in dollars at $1,199-$2,499 per plan; a medical concierge charges Rs 2-3 lakh a year.
In the US, caregivers spend about $7,200 a year out of pocket, and employed caregivers report nearly $1,000 a month.
No source gives what NRIs spend on coordination software specifically.
In the NRI segment the child abroad pays and stays the decision-maker; Anvayaa's early customers were almost entirely NRIs, and attendants are paid from NRO accounts.
In the US, the payer for coordination services has shifted to employers and insurers: Wellthy moved from direct-to-consumer to employer-paid and no longer promotes private pay.
Many US employers (Dow, Medtronic, Philadelphia, MIT, Stanford, Yale and others) already buy caregiving benefits from Wellthy, Cariloop or Bright Horizons.
Indian employers also buy elder care as a benefit (Anvayaa's Nischint plan).
Coordination problems are widely described (fragmented WhatsApp updates, sibling conflict over appointments and aides, coordination challenges in a 2,000-caregiver survey).
No source measures how often tasks are missed or communication breaks down; frequency stays unquantified.
India: Emoha, Anvayaa, Samarth, Apollo NRI 360, Healync and newer entrants (Nila, ParentPulse) serve NRI families, mostly as human-led care-manager services with apps attached.
Anvayaa's FY25 revenue was Rs 14.6 crore after a decade, suggesting a modest market for NRI elder-care subscriptions.
US: employer-paid Wellthy, Cariloop, ianacare and Bright Horizons already include sibling care circles, medication tracking and shared coordination hubs; free tools like Lotsa Helping Hands exist.
Caregiver tech adoption has historically been low (7% in AARP's 2016 study; 9% use scheduling assistants in 2026).
No evidence was found on why families switch providers.
